paragraphs.heading: What a galaxy is
paragraphs.text: A galaxy is a system of stars, planetary systems, the remains of stars, gas, dust and dark matter, all held together by gravity. The name comes from a Greek word meaning milky, a nod to the Milky Way, the galaxy that holds our Solar System. Most of a typical galaxy's mass is dark matter, and stars and nebulae make up only a few percent of it. Supermassive black holes are a common feature at galactic centers.

paragraphs.heading: Sizes and numbers
paragraphs.text: Galaxies hold about 100 million stars on average, but they range from dwarfs with under a thousand stars to supergiants with one hundred trillion. Each of those stars orbits its galaxy's center of mass. Most galaxies are 1,000 to 100,000 parsecs across, roughly 3,000 to 300,000 light years. The Milky Way is at least 26,800 parsecs wide, and Andromeda, its nearest large neighbour, lies just over 750,000 parsecs away. Estimates put the count in the observable universe between 200 billion and 2 trillion.

paragraphs.heading: Shapes and groups
paragraphs.text: Astronomers sort galaxies by how they look: elliptical, spiral or irregular. The Milky Way is a spiral. Some galaxies stand out for other reasons, such as interacting with another galaxy, forming stars at an unusual pace, or hosting an active galactic nucleus. Most galaxies are bound by gravity into groups, clusters and superclusters; ours belongs to the Local Group, which it dominates together with Andromeda, inside the Virgo Supercluster. On the largest scale, these gatherings form sheets and filaments around immense voids.

paragraphs.heading: Island universes
paragraphs.text: Galaxies were first spotted through telescopes and called spiral nebulae. Most astronomers of the 18th and 19th centuries saw them as unresolved star clusters or as extragalactic nebulae, and what they really were stayed a mystery. Larger telescopes later broke a few bright nearby ones, such as Andromeda, into vast crowds of stars, and their faintness placed them far beyond the Milky Way. People began calling them island universes. Harlow Shapley pushed for the word galaxy, but the influential Edwin Hubble kept saying nebulae, and the naming did not fully change until after Hubble died in 1953.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping our own galaxy
paragraphs.text: The Greek philosopher Democritus suggested that the bright band of the Milky Way might be made of distant stars. Galileo gave proof in 1610, when his telescope showed it held a huge number of faint stars. In 1750 Thomas Wright guessed it was a rotating body of stars bound by gravity, seen as a band because we look out from inside its disk. Later, Kapteyn and Harlow Shapley drew very different maps: one put the Sun near the center of a small galaxy, the other far from the center of a wide flat disk. Both ignored how dust dims light, and the modern picture came only after Robert Julius Trumpler measured that effect in 1930.

paragraphs.heading: Naming them
paragraphs.text: Millions of galaxies have been catalogued, but only a handful have well-known names, like Andromeda, the Magellanic Clouds, the Whirlpool and the Sombrero. Astronomers work with numbers from catalogues such as Messier's and the NGC, and each well-known galaxy carries a different number in every catalogue that lists it. The spiral Messier 109, for example, is also NGC 3992 and UGC 6937. A few galaxies beyond our own can be seen on a dark night with the unaided eye, including Andromeda, both Magellanic Clouds and the Triangulum Galaxy.
